title: Functions: Packaging a Behaviour
description: Once a piece of logic earns a name, you can talk about it, reuse it, and read your own program at a glance.

content.value: def avoid_obstacle(): wraps a whole block of logic behind one name. Anywhere you'd otherwise repeat those same lines, you instead just write avoid_obstacle() — call the name, and everything inside runs.

Compare that while True: line to Module 10's earlier ones: it used to contain the whole decision. Now it just says what's happening in plain English — avoid_obstacle() — and the details live inside the function, one level down. That's the real value of a function: it lets the top of your program read like a summary.

content.title: 🐍 Package it yourself
content.hint: Define a function called avoid_obstacle() containing the distance check, then call it from inside a while True: loop.

content.value: Just like robot.forward(speed=50) takes a parameter, your own functions can too: def turn_away(angle): would let you write turn_away(45) in one spot and turn_away(90) in another, reusing the same logic with different specifics each time.

This is exactly the same idea as ARIA's own robot object: robot.forward, robot.distance and every other method are themselves just functions, packaged up and given names, sitting inside one object instead of floating free in your program.
Key takeaway: a function packages a chunk of logic behind a name, so the rest of your program can call it by that name instead of repeating the details — making a long program read like a short one.

quiz.question: What does `def avoid_obstacle():` actually do?
options: Defines a name for a block of logic, without running it yet — it only runs when called
quiz.explain: Definition and execution are separate steps. `def` just creates the function; calling `avoid_obstacle()` is what actually runs it.

quiz.question: What's the main benefit of writing `while True: avoid_obstacle()` instead of putting the whole distance-check logic directly inside the loop?
options: The loop reads as a plain-English summary of what's happening, with the details tucked inside the function
quiz.explain: Naming a behaviour lets the calling code stay short and readable, while the implementation detail lives one level down.
